blocks.body:
Two questions about spaces of continuous functions come up again and again in analysis. First: in $\mathbb{R}^n$ every bounded sequence has a convergent subsequence; when does a sequence of functions have a uniformly convergent subsequence? Second: polynomials are the functions we can actually compute with; which continuous functions can be approximated uniformly by them, or by other simple families?

The Arzelà–Ascoli theorem answers the first: boundedness is not enough, but boundedness plus a uniform control on oscillation (equicontinuity) is. The Stone–Weierstrass theorem answers the second: on a compact set, any algebra of functions that contains the constants and separates points can approximate every continuous function. Both are statements about the [[compactness|compact sets]] and the dense subsets of the space $C(K)$ with the sup norm.

blocks.title: Bounded sequences of functions need not converge
blocks.body:
Throughout, $K$ is a compact metric space (often $[a,b]$) and $C(K)$ is the set of continuous real functions on $K$ with distance $\|f - g\|_\infty = \max_{x \in K}|f(x) - g(x)|$. Convergence in this distance is [[uniform-convergence]], and $C(K)$ is complete.

Bounded is not enough. The functions $f_n(x) = x^n$ on $[0,1]$ all satisfy $|f_n| \le 1$. Their pointwise limit is $0$ for $x < 1$ and $1$ at $x = 1$, which is discontinuous; since a uniform limit of continuous functions is continuous, and any subsequence has the same pointwise limit, no subsequence converges uniformly. Quantitatively, $f_n(x) - f_{2n}(x) = t - t^2$ with $t = x^n$, whose maximum over $[0,1]$ is $1/4$ (at $x^n = 1/2$). The functions get steeper and steeper near $x = 1$; the missing ingredient is a bound on steepness that is the same for all of them.

blocks.title: Uniformly bounded and equicontinuous
blocks.body:
A family $\mathcal{F} \subseteq C(K)$ is

- uniformly bounded if there is $M$ with $|f(x)| \le M$ for all $f \in \mathcal{F}$ and $x \in K$;
- equicontinuous if for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there is $\delta > 0$ such that $d(x,y) < \delta$ implies $|f(x) - f(y)| < \varepsilon$ for all $f \in \mathcal{F}$ at once.

The point is that one $\delta$ works for every member of the family. The commonest example: all functions that are Lipschitz with the same constant $L$ form an equicontinuous family (take $\delta = \varepsilon/L$), so, for instance, any family of differentiable functions on $[a,b]$ with $|f'| \le L$ is equicontinuous by the [[mvt|mean value theorem]].

blocks.title: Arzelà–Ascoli theorem
blocks.body: Let $K$ be a compact metric space and $\mathcal{F} \subseteq C(K)$. Then every sequence in $\mathcal{F}$ has a subsequence converging uniformly on $K$ (to a function in $C(K)$) if and only if $\mathcal{F}$ is uniformly bounded and equicontinuous. Equivalently, $\mathcal{F}$ has compact closure in $C(K)$ if and only if it is uniformly bounded and equicontinuous.

We prove the direction used in applications: uniformly bounded and equicontinuous implies a uniformly convergent subsequence. Let $(f_n)$ be a sequence in $\mathcal{F}$ with $|f_n| \le M$.

Step 1: a countable dense set. For each $m \ge 1$, compactness gives finitely many points such that every $x \in K$ is within $1/m$ of one of them. Let $D = \{d_1, d_2, \dots\}$ be the union over all $m$ of these finite sets; it is countable and dense.

Step 2: convergence on $D$ by a diagonal argument. The numbers $f_n(d_1)$ lie in $[-M,M]$, so by Bolzano–Weierstrass some subsequence $(f_{1,n})$ converges at $d_1$. From it extract a subsequence $(f_{2,n})$ converging at $d_2$, and so on. The diagonal sequence $g_n = f_{n,n}$ is, from the $j$-th term on, a subsequence of $(f_{j,n})$, so $g_n(d_j)$ converges for every $j$.

Step 3: equicontinuity upgrades this to uniform convergence. Let $\varepsilon > 0$ and choose $\delta$ from equicontinuity. Pick $m$ with $1/m < \delta$, and let $E \subseteq D$ be the finite $1/m$-net from step 1. Since $E$ is finite, there is $N$ with $|g_n(e) - g_k(e)| < \varepsilon$ for all $e \in E$ and $n, k \ge N$. For any $x \in K$ choose $e \in E$ with $d(x,e) < 1/m < \delta$; then for $n, k \ge N$

$$|g_n(x) - g_k(x)| \le |g_n(x) - g_n(e)| + |g_n(e) - g_k(e)| + |g_k(e) - g_k(x)| < 3\varepsilon.$$

So $(g_n)$ is uniformly Cauchy, and since $C(K)$ is complete it converges uniformly to a continuous function.

For the converse, suppose every sequence in $\mathcal{F}$ has a uniformly convergent subsequence, so the closure of $\mathcal{F}$ is compact. A compact set in a metric space is bounded, which gives uniform boundedness. Given $\varepsilon$, compactness gives finitely many $h_1, \dots, h_r \in C(K)$ such that each $f \in \mathcal{F}$ has $\|f - h_i\|_\infty < \varepsilon$ for some $i$. Each $h_i$ is uniformly continuous on compact $K$; take $\delta$ that works for all $h_i$ with $\varepsilon$. Then $|f(x) - f(y)| < 3\varepsilon$ whenever $d(x,y) < \delta$, which is equicontinuity.

blocks.title: What Arzelà–Ascoli is used for
blocks.body:
Arzelà–Ascoli is the standard way of producing solutions as limits. Three typical uses:

- Peano's theorem. For $y' = f(t,y)$ with $f$ merely continuous, Euler polygon approximations all have slope at most $\max|f|$, so they are equi-Lipschitz; a subsequence converges uniformly, and the limit solves the equation. Existence holds without the Lipschitz condition needed in [[contraction-mapping|Picard's theorem]] (but uniqueness may fail).
- Integral operators. If $k$ is continuous on $[0,1]^2$, the operator $Tf(x) = \int_0^1 k(x,y)f(y)\,dy$ sends the unit ball of $C[0,1]$ into a uniformly bounded, equicontinuous family (because $k$ is uniformly continuous), so $T$ maps bounded sets to sets with compact closure: it is a [[compact-operators|compact operator]].
- Normal families. In complex analysis, Montel's theorem says a locally bounded family of holomorphic functions has a subsequence converging uniformly on compact sets; the Cauchy estimates supply equicontinuity. This is a key step in proving the Riemann mapping theorem ([[conformal-maps]]).

blocks.title: Approximating by polynomials: Bernstein's idea
blocks.body:
Now the approximation question. Given a continuous $f$ on $[0,1]$, Bernstein's construction is

$$B_nf(x) = \sum_{k=0}^n f\!\left(\frac kn\right)\binom nk x^k(1-x)^{n-k}.$$

There is a probabilistic reading ([[distributions]]): if $S$ counts the successes in $n$ independent trials with success probability $x$, then $B_nf(x) = \mathbb{E}\,f(S/n)$. Since $S/n$ concentrates near $x$ when $n$ is large (its variance is $x(1-x)/n$), we expect $B_nf(x) \to f(x)$.

For $f(x) = |x - \tfrac12|$, the largest error $\|B_nf - f\|_\infty$ is attained at $x = 1/2$ and equals about $0.1230$ for $n = 10$, $0.0398$ for $n = 100$ and $0.0126$ for $n = 1000$: convergence, but slowly, at roughly the rate $1/\sqrt{2\pi n}$.

blocks.title: Weierstrass approximation theorem
blocks.body: For every continuous $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ and every $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a polynomial $p$ with $|f(x) - p(x)| < \varepsilon$ for all $x \in [a,b]$. On $[0,1]$ one may take $p = B_nf$ for $n$ large.

By a linear change of variable we may take $[a,b] = [0,1]$. Write $p_k(x) = \binom nk x^k(1-x)^{n-k}$. The binomial theorem and its derivatives give the three identities

$$\sum_k p_k(x) = 1,\qquad \sum_k \frac kn\,p_k(x) = x,\qquad \sum_k\left(\frac kn - x\right)^2 p_k(x) = \frac{x(1-x)}{n}.$$

Let $M = \|f\|_\infty$ and $\varepsilon > 0$. Since $f$ is uniformly continuous on $[0,1]$, there is $\delta > 0$ with $|f(s) - f(x)| < \varepsilon$ whenever $|s - x| < \delta$. Using the first identity,

$$|B_nf(x) - f(x)| \le \sum_k \left|f\!\left(\frac kn\right) - f(x)\right| p_k(x).$$

Split the sum. Terms with $|k/n - x| < \delta$ contribute less than $\varepsilon\sum_k p_k = \varepsilon$. For the others, $|f(k/n) - f(x)| \le 2M \le 2M(k/n - x)^2/\delta^2$, so by the third identity they contribute at most $\frac{2M}{\delta^2}\cdot\frac{x(1-x)}{n} \le \frac{M}{2\delta^2 n}$. Hence $\|B_nf - f\|_\infty \le \varepsilon + \frac{M}{2\delta^2 n} < 2\varepsilon$ once $n > M/(2\delta^2\varepsilon)$.

blocks.title: Stone–Weierstrass theorem
blocks.body:
Let $K$ be a compact Hausdorff space (for example a compact metric space) and $\mathcal{A} \subseteq C(K, \mathbb{R})$ a subalgebra (closed under sums, products and real scalar multiples) such that

1. $\mathcal{A}$ contains the constant functions, and
2. $\mathcal{A}$ separates points: for $x \ne y$ in $K$ there is $g \in \mathcal{A}$ with $g(x) \ne g(y)$.

Then $\mathcal{A}$ is dense in $C(K,\mathbb{R})$ for the sup norm. For complex-valued functions the same holds if, in addition, $\mathcal{A}$ is closed under complex conjugation.

blocks.title: Why Stone–Weierstrass is true, and what it gives
blocks.body:
Proof sketch, for the curious. Let $\overline{\mathcal{A}}$ be the uniform closure, again an algebra. (i) If $g \in \overline{\mathcal{A}}$ then $|g| \in \overline{\mathcal{A}}$: apply Weierstrass to approximate $t \mapsto |t|$ by polynomials on $[-\|g\|, \|g\|]$, and compose. (ii) Hence $\max(g,h) = \tfrac12(g + h + |g-h|)$ and $\min(g,h)$ are in $\overline{\mathcal{A}}$. (iii) Separation plus constants give, for any $x \ne y$ and any target values $\alpha, \beta$, a function in $\mathcal{A}$ with value $\alpha$ at $x$ and $\beta$ at $y$. (iv) Given $f$ and $\varepsilon$, fix $x$; for each $y$ take $h_y$ matching $f$ at $x$ and $y$; finitely many of the open sets $\{h_y < f + \varepsilon\}$ cover $K$, and the minimum of those $h_y$ is below $f + \varepsilon$ everywhere and equals $f(x)$ at $x$. Taking a maximum of finitely many such functions over different $x$ (again by compactness) produces an element of $\overline{\mathcal{A}}$ within $\varepsilon$ of $f$.

Special cases worth knowing: polynomials in $n$ variables are dense in $C(K)$ for any compact $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$; trigonometric polynomials $\sum_{|k| \le N} c_ke^{ikx}$ are dense in the continuous $2\pi$-periodic functions (functions on the circle), which is the uniform side of [[fourier-series]].

blocks.title: Testing equicontinuity
blocks.body: Which of these families on $[0,\pi]$ are equicontinuous? (a) $\{\sin(nx) : n \ge 1\}$; (b) $\{\sin(x + n) : n \ge 1\}$; (c) $\{\sin(nx)/n : n \ge 1\}$. For each equicontinuous one, what does Arzelà–Ascoli give?
blocks.solution:
(a) Not equicontinuous. Take $\varepsilon = 1/2$. For any $\delta > 0$ choose $n$ with $\pi/(2n) < \delta$: the points $0$ and $\pi/(2n)$ are within $\delta$, but $|\sin(n\cdot\tfrac{\pi}{2n}) - \sin 0| = 1$.

(b) Equicontinuous: each function has derivative bounded by $1$, so all are $1$-Lipschitz; they are bounded by $1$. Arzelà–Ascoli says some subsequence converges uniformly. Indeed, the numbers $n \bmod 2\pi$ lie in $[0, 2\pi]$, so some subsequence $n_j \bmod 2\pi$ converges to some $c$, and then $\sin(x + n_j) \to \sin(x + c)$ uniformly.

(c) Equicontinuous: $|(\sin nx/n)'| = |\cos nx| \le 1$. Here the whole sequence converges uniformly, to $0$, since $|\sin(nx)/n| \le 1/n$.

blocks.title: Bernstein polynomials of x²
blocks.body: Compute $B_nf$ for $f(x) = x^2$ and find $\|B_nf - f\|_\infty$ exactly.
blocks.solution:
$B_nf(x) = \sum_k (k/n)^2p_k(x) = \mathbb{E}[(S/n)^2]$ where $S$ is binomial with parameters $n$ and $x$. Since $\mathbb{E}[S/n] = x$ and $\operatorname{Var}(S/n) = x(1-x)/n$,

$$B_nf(x) = x^2 + \frac{x(1-x)}{n}.$$

The error $x(1-x)/n$ is largest at $x = 1/2$, so $\|B_nf - f\|_\infty = \frac{1}{4n}$. Bernstein polynomials converge, but even for a polynomial they converge only at rate $1/n$; their virtue is simplicity and the fact that they preserve positivity and monotonicity, not speed.

blocks.title: Moments and even polynomials
blocks.body:
(a) Let $f$ be continuous on $[0,1]$ with $\int_0^1 f(x)x^n\,dx = 0$ for every $n = 0, 1, 2, \ldots$. Prove $f \equiv 0$.

(b) Are the even polynomials $c_0 + c_1x^2 + \cdots + c_mx^{2m}$ dense in $C[0,1]$? In $C[-1,1]$?
blocks.solution:
(a) By linearity $\int_0^1 fp = 0$ for every polynomial $p$. By Weierstrass choose polynomials $p_k \to f$ uniformly. Then

$$\int_0^1 f^2\,dx = \int_0^1 f(f - p_k)\,dx \le \|f\|_\infty\,\|f - p_k\|_\infty \to 0,$$

so $\int_0^1 f^2 = 0$, and since $f^2$ is continuous and non-negative, $f \equiv 0$.

(b) The even polynomials form an algebra containing the constants. On $[0,1]$, the function $x^2$ separates points ($x^2 \ne y^2$ for $x \ne y \ge 0$), so by Stone–Weierstrass they are dense in $C[0,1]$. On $[-1,1]$ every even polynomial takes the same value at $x$ and $-x$, so separation fails; uniform limits of even functions are even, so a function like $x$ cannot be approximated. The closure is exactly the even continuous functions (apply the $[0,1]$ result to $g(\sqrt{t})$).

blocks.body:
- Compactness of the domain matters. On $\mathbb{R}$, $f_n(x) = \sin(x/n)$ is uniformly bounded and equicontinuous (all $1$-Lipschitz) and tends to $0$ pointwise, but $\|f_n\|_\infty = 1$ for every $n$, so no subsequence converges uniformly to $0$ (or to anything else, since the pointwise limit is $0$). On non-compact domains one gets only uniform convergence on compact subsets.
- Equicontinuity at each point separately is weaker in general; on a compact domain it implies the uniform version used above, by the same argument that continuous functions on compact sets are uniformly continuous.
- Stone–Weierstrass needs the constants (or at least an algebra that vanishes at no common point): the polynomials with $p(0) = 0$ are not dense in $C[0,1]$, since they all vanish at $0$.
- In the complex case conjugation is essential. Polynomials in $z$ separate points of the unit circle and contain constants, but $\bar z$ cannot be approximated uniformly there: $\oint p(z)\,dz = 0$ for every polynomial, while $\oint \bar z\,dz = 2\pi i$.
- Uniform approximation by polynomials is not the same as convergence of Taylor series: $f(x) = |x|$ has no Taylor series at $0$ but is a uniform limit of polynomials on $[-1,1]$.

Arzelà–Ascoli characterises the [[compactness|compact]] subsets of $C(K)$ and is how one proves existence: Peano's theorem for ODEs, the compactness of integral operators in the theory of [[compact-operators]] and the Fredholm alternative, and, via Montel's theorem on normal families, the Riemann mapping theorem in [[conformal-maps]]. Stone–Weierstrass makes polynomials and trigonometric polynomials dense, which is the starting point for [[fourier-series]], polynomial [[interpolation-quadrature|interpolation and quadrature]], and for showing that continuous functions are dense in [[lp-spaces]]. Both theorems are classic illustrations of how [[uniform-convergence]] and compactness interact.

1. Show that the family $$\{f \in C^1[0,1] : f(0) = 0,\ \int_0^1 f'(x)^2\,dx \le 1\}$$ is uniformly bounded and equicontinuous. (Hint: Cauchy–Schwarz gives $|f(x) - f(y)| \le \sqrt{|x - y|}$.)
2. Is $\{x^n : n \ge 1\}$ equicontinuous on $[0, 1/2]$? On $[0,1]$? Justify both answers.
3. Show that functions of the form $\sum_{j=1}^m c_je^{-a_jx}$ with $a_j \ge 0$ are dense in $C[0,1]$.
4. Let $f \in C[0,1]$ and suppose $\int_0^1 f(x)e^{nx}\,dx = 0$ for all integers $n \ge 0$. Prove that $f \equiv 0$.
